title: Find the Equation with My Numbers
description: Build one realistic set of values from a word problem, then test every answer choice to identify the equation that always matches the context.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep what you tried, even if you got stuck. You can continue without submitting an answer.

  1. \(t=\frac{3ab}{2(a+b)}\)
  2. \(t=\frac{2(a+b)}{3ab}\)
  3. \(t=\frac{2ab}{3(a+b)}\)
  4. \(t=\frac{2ab}{a+b}\)

shared_prompt.title: Two hoses filling a tank
shared_prompt.html:
One hose can fill an empty tank in \(a\) hours, and another can fill it in \(b\) hours. Each runs at a constant rate, and \(a,b>0\).

The tank is already one-third full when both hoses are turned on. They finish filling it together in \(t\) hours. Which equation relates \(a,b,t\)?

blocks.html:
Build one filling story

The hose question combines two rates and a partly filled tank. Writing a general equation means working with several fractions.

Find the Equation lets you build one easy numerical situation and test which equation describes it. We’ll start with a simpler membership fee, then return to the tank.

shared_prompt.title: Gym membership
shared_prompt.html: A gym charges a one-time sign-up fee of $15 and $8 for each month. Let \(m\) be the number of months and \(c\) be the total cost.

blocks.html:
Build a membership example

Choose 4 months. At $8 per month plus a $15 sign-up fee, the total is $47. Record \(m=4,c=47\), then test the choices.

content.prompt: Which equation is true when \(m=4\) and \(c=47\)?
content.hint: Put \(4\) everywhere you see \(m\). Which right side equals \(47\)?
content.explanation: \(8(4)+15=47\), so \(c=8m+15\) agrees with the membership you built.

blocks.html:
Your example tests a claim

An equation describing the story must be true for every possible situation in it. If it fails for your legal example, eliminate it. If several choices work, try a different example.

Build, Record, Test

  1. Set the equations aside.
  2. Choose a legal starting value and build the rest from the story.
  3. Record the complete set.
  4. Test every equation with that same set.
  5. Rebuild and retest a tie.

Choose a starting quantity

For five more red objects than blue objects, choose 10 blue objects. That forces 15 red objects. Choosing both counts independently could break the story.

content.prompt: A theater sold \(7\) fewer premium tickets than standard tickets. If you choose \(s=20\) standard tickets, which value must you use for the number \(p\) of premium tickets?
content.hint: Premium is the smaller quantity: take \(7\) away from \(20\).
content.explanation: The story forces \(p=20-7=13\), so the legal value set is \((s,p)=(20,13)\).

blocks.html:
Keep the complete set in view

For the theater example, record \(s=20,p=13\). Reuse those values in every choice so the equations all face the same test.

shared_prompt.title: Museum ticket revenue
shared_prompt.html: A museum charges $18 for each adult ticket and $11 for each student ticket. Let \(a\) be the number of adult tickets, \(s\) the number of student tickets, and \(r\) the total revenue.

blocks.html:
Build two groups and their total

Choose 2 adult tickets and 3 student tickets. The revenue is \(2(18)+3(11)=69\). Record \(a=2,s=3,r=69\) before testing the equations.

content.prompt: Which equation is true for \(a=2\), \(s=3\), and \(r=69\)?
content.hint: Substitute all three recorded values. The correct right side must equal \(69\).
content.explanation: \(18(2)+11(3)=69\), so \(r=18a+11s\) tells the truth about your museum purchase.

blocks.html:
Picture “fewer than” first

Six fewer shrubs than flowers means 20 flowers would go with 14 shrubs. Use that concrete pair to test direction instead of deciding from the equation’s appearance.

content.prompt: A garden has \(6\) fewer shrubs than flowers. You choose \(f=20\) flowers, so \(s=14\) shrubs. Which equation agrees with your values?
content.hint: Substitute \(f=20\) and \(s=14\) into each equation; do not rely on the order of the words.
content.explanation: \(14=20-6\), so \(s=f-6\). The numbers reveal the direction without a translation rule.

blocks.html:
Build a rate example

At 12 liters per minute, 5 minutes gives 60 liters. Record \(t=5,v=60\), then test the equations with those units and values.

content.prompt: Water flows at \(12\) liters per minute. Let \(t\) be minutes and \(v\) be liters. Which equation is true for \(t=5\) and \(v=60\)?
content.hint: Test \(t=5\) and \(v=60\). Which statement becomes true?

shared_prompt.title: Hardcover books
shared_prompt.html: A bookstore says 35% of its books are hardcover. Let \(b\) be the total number of books and \(h\) the number of hardcover books.

blocks.html:
Make the percent easy

If 35% of the books are hardcover, choose 200 books. That gives 70 hardcover books. Record \(b=200,h=70\) and test the choices.

content.prompt: Which equation is true for \(b=200\) total books and \(h=70\) hardcover books?
content.hint: Substitute \(200\) for \(b\) and \(70\) for \(h\). Check which equality is true.

blocks.html:
Keep the arithmetic easy

Use a friendly percent base, small counts, or multiples of a ratio. The values must describe a possible situation and satisfy every condition.

Respect the problem’s limits

Counts must be whole numbers; required positive quantities must stay positive. Keep any stated minimum, maximum, total, or ordering true in your example.

content.prompt: A tournament has a positive whole number \(n\) of teams, and \(n\ge4\). Which is a legal, convenient choice for \(n\)?
content.hint: The value must be a whole number, positive, and at least \(4\).
content.explanation: \(6\) satisfies every stated condition and is easy to use.

shared_prompt.title: Two equations that match one value
shared_prompt.html:
\(y\) is 2 more than twice \(x\). Which candidate equation describes that relationship?

  • \(y=2x+2\)
  • \(y=4x\)

blocks.html:
Two equations can tie

For this relationship, \(x=1\) gives \(y=4\). Both \(y=2x+2\) and \(y=4x\) happen to be true there. That example does not distinguish the choices.

content.prompt: Two candidate equations are true for your first legal value set. What should you do next?
choices: Pick whichever tied equation is written with fewer symbols.
Build a different legal value set and retest only the tied equations.
Change one variable separately inside each tied equation.
Conclude that both tied equations describe the story's relationship.
content.hint: One example did not separate the choices, so create new evidence from the same story.
content.explanation: A second legal situation breaks an accidental tie without requiring you to translate the equations.

blocks.html:
Rebuild from a new starting value

Choose \(x=3\). The story gives \(y=8\). Now \(y=2x+2\) works and \(y=4x\) fails. Recalculate dependent values whenever you change the starting value.

Use a supplied example

If the story already provides a complete value set, test it directly. If it fixes a total, your example must also have that total; do not choose all the parts independently.

shared_prompt.title: Delivery fees
shared_prompt.html: A delivery company charges $9 to start an order, $2.50 per pound, and $4 for insurance. Let \(w\) be the package weight in pounds and \(t\) be the total charge.

blocks.html:
Include every part of the charge

For the insured package, choose a weight and calculate its full charge from the story. Test the equations using that weight and total.

A rearranged equation can still work

If q is 5 more than p, the pair \(p=12,q=17\) makes both \(q=p+5\) and \(q-p=5\) true. Test the equality rather than rejecting an unfamiliar arrangement.

Return to the two hoses

Try the opening question again. Build a possible filling situation before comparing the equations.

content.prompt: Which equation describes the filling time?
content.hint: Choose hose times that make the fractions easy. Work out how much both hoses fill in one hour and how much of the tank is still empty; test the same complete situation in every equation.
content.solution:
Choose \(a=2,\ b=6\) hours.
In one hour the hoses fill \(1/2+1/6=2/3\) of the tank. Exactly \(2/3\) is still empty, so \(t=1\) hour.
Using \(a=2,b=6\), choices A–D give \(9/4,\ 4/9,\ 1,\ 3\) hours.
Only C agrees with your story: \(t=2ab/[3(a+b)]\).
content.explanation: C works. Your example gave a one-hour filling time, and only that equation matched the same hose times and starting amount.

content.prompt: A friend texts you a Find the Equation question. Without checking the lesson, what do you tell them to do — start to finish?
choices: Read the equations first; build one legal value set from the story; test only the two closest choices; rebuild if both fail.
Ignore the story; build and record one legal value set from the equations; test every choice with it; accept the first that works.
Ignore the equations; build a new legal value set for each choice; test each choice with its own values; retest if choices tie.
Ignore the equations; build and record one legal value set from the story; test every choice with it; rebuild and retest if choices tie.
content.explanation: You have it. The story creates the evidence, every equation faces the same evidence, and a second legal example resolves an accidental tie.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: Which equation represents the insured package charge?
content.explanation: \(2.5(4)+13=23\). The \(13\) combines the $9 start fee and $4 insurance charge.

content.prompt: A cafe sells drip coffee for $2.75 per cup and cold brew for $4.25 per cup. It sells c cups of drip coffee and b cups of cold brew for a total of R dollars. Which equation represents this situation?
content.explanation: Choose, for example, c=2 and b=4. The story gives R=22.50. Only \(2.75c+4.25b=R\) is true for that complete value set.

content.html:
Story first, equations second

Build the values from the story and test each equation against them.
